persona.who: 49, IT services manager in Pune, 22 years in the same company, laid off last month. Daughter in 11th, home loan, aging mother.
persona.note: twenty two years in one company and they let me go in a 10 minute call. I have not told my mother. Every morning I still wake up at 6 like I have to go to office.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call fear of what might happen, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the shock and the shame, named without judgement.

understanding.mirror: Twenty-two years and a ten-minute call. Every morning you wake at six and your body still expects the office.
understanding.insight: It is not the layoff that keeps you awake. It is the sentence you are still passing on yourself in the silence, as if the call was a verdict on who you are.

queries.hook: The shock of being let go after two decades, and the shame of not being able to tell the person who raised you. I lost my job.
queries.diagnose: When a result goes wrong, the mind turns against itself; self-blame grows from believing the outcome alone measures our worth.
queries.steady: A failure is something that happened, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; learn what this taught you, make amends where you can, and begin again.
queries.story: A man who lost everything he built shows you what rising again looks like from the inside.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: how the world treats someone who has lost money.
verse.sanskrit: तानीन्द्रियाण्यविकलानि तदेव नाम सा बुद्धिरप्रतिहता वचनं तदेव । अर्थोष्मणा विरहितः पुरुषः क्षणेन सोऽप्यन्य एव भवतीति विचित्रमेतत् ॥
verse.line: Same person, same mind, same voice. Lose money, and people suddenly treat you as someone else.
verse.translation: The same faculties, unimpaired; the same name; the same unclouded mind; the same speech. Yet a man deprived of the warmth of wealth becomes, in a moment, someone else. How strange!
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.
verse.misuse: The verse mocks how the world sees you; it does not measure your worth.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari writes to the reader from a quiet place of observation. He speaks of a man who has lost his money. The man still has the same mind, the same voice, the same name. Yet in a moment, the world treats him as a different person. He sees that the warmth of wealth was not his own. It was a borrowed light, and now it has gone cold.
verse.for_you: The ten-minute call took the money, not the person. You still wake at six with the same mind that built twenty-two years at one company. That mind has not changed. The silence after the call is loud, but it is not a verdict on who you are.

verse.speaker: Janaka
verse.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
verse.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
verse.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
verse.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
verse.why: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.
verse.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.

prasang.title: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.story_hook: One spring morning, a king out for a walk overheard a song that he could not stop thinking about.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

verse.meaning: King Janaka is alone on his palace roof. He has just heard wandering sages singing about the self, and he questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away. He gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clings. The verse says that dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are great calamities. And misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, become a kind of fortune. The mind that clutches what it has turns good into trouble.
verse.for_you: You wake at six and still go through the motions of a life that is not there. The silence of the morning is where the verdict lands. Let the mind that woke up with you now accept the quiet. It does not mean you stop looking.

verse.speaker: Ribhu
verse.setting: Ribhu on people of steady goodness.
verse.sanskrit: नापदि ग्लानिमायान्ति निशि हेमाम्बुजं यथा । नेहन्ते प्रकृतादन्यद्रमन्ते शिष्टवर्त्मनि ॥
verse.line: Good people do not wilt in hard times, like a golden lotus that stays open at night.
verse.translation: In adversity they do not wilt, as the golden lotus does not close at night. They want nothing beyond what is at hand and delight in the path of the good.
verse.why: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

prasang.title: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

verse.for_you: The call ended in ten minutes, and now the silence is where the trouble lives. Your parents are far away and growing older, and the future is a blank. Let the next hour be just the next hour. Do not ask it to be anything more than it is.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari is writing to you, someone who has just been struck down. He says a ball knocked down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last. He is not saying the pain is small or that it will vanish. He is saying this is not the end of the game. The ball is still in the air. It has not been lost.
verse.for_you: You still wake at six. That habit is the ball. It is the part of you that knows how to stand. Hold that, and let the rest wait.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
verse.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help'. Arjuna himself asks for help; this is about not abandoning yourself.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.for_you: Do what you can today, take refuge in what does not change, and meet each moment with courage instead of rehearsing the worst.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying on the ground, defeated and refusing to rise after losing his kingdom. She tells him not to hold himself in contempt or accept a life of little. She asks him to set his mind on what is truly good and to stop fearing. She means that past failure does not define a person. The results of any action are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed. You have lived twenty-two years at one company. That is not nothing.
verse.for_you: You still wake at six. Let that body carry you to the kitchen. Make a cup of tea and sit with it for five minutes. Do not plan the next week. Just let your mind rest on one small thing that is truly yours, not the company's.

story.title: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
story.story_hook: The prince who had everything came back from his travels and stopped laughing.
story.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
story.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

anchor.speaker: Rama's attendant
anchor.setting: Rama's attendants tell King Dasharatha how the prince has changed since his pilgrimage.
anchor.sanskrit: रामो राजीवपत्राक्षो यतःप्रभृति चागतः । सविप्रस्तीर्थयात्रायास्ततःप्रभृति दुर्मनाः ॥
anchor.line: Ever since he came back from the trip, he hasn't been himself.
anchor.translation: Ever since lotus-eyed Rama came back from his pilgrimage with the brahmins, he has been low in spirit.
anchor.why: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.

story.hook_title: Rama came home from his pilgrimage and stopped laughing
story.teaser: Rama came home from his pilgrimage and stopped laughing
story.for_you: You are sitting in that silence after the call, the way Rama sat alone. You are not broken because you are still. You are simply asking the first real questions of a life that has been running on someone else's track.

script: You are still waking at six. The alarm is not for an office you no longer enter. You are carrying a sentence you have not spoken aloud. Someone told you to your face that your work was finished. In ten minutes, they took away the money.

Bhartrihari watches from a quiet place. He sees a man who wakes one morning without gold in his purse. The man still has his mind, his voice, his name. But the world steps back. The same people who bowed now look through him. And Bhartrihari asks the reader: how strange it is that a man becomes someone else in a single moment. Bhartrihari said:
तानीन्द्रियाण्यविकलानि तदेव नाम सा बुद्धिरप्रतिहता वचनं तदेव, अर्थोष्मणा विरहितः पुरुषः क्षणेन सोऽप्यन्य एव भवतीति विचित्रमेतत्.
In plain words: Same person, same mind, same voice. Lose money, and people suddenly treat you as someone else.

This is what money does. It is a borrowed light. It makes the world treat you as someone else, even though your mind is the same. The verse does not say you are less. It says the warmth belonged to the gold, not to you. You are still the person who built twenty-two years. The loss is real. The silence is real. But the man inside the loss is exactly who he was before the call.

Sit with your morning coffee. Let it be warm in your hands. Notice that the world has not changed, only the money. The silence is loud, but your mind is still your own. Let it rest in that truth for a moment before the day begins.
The money left, not the mind.

depth.life: The silence after the call is loud. You still wake at six as if the office exists. You feel the shift in how the world might look at you now, and the shame of it sits heavy in your chest. The money is gone, but the mind that built twenty-two years is still there.
depth.points: The verse points out that the world changes its tune when wealth leaves. It is not your mind or your name that changed. The coldness you sense is in the air around you, not in the person you are. Your worth is not measured by the warmth of money.
depth.practice: Sit with your morning coffee and name one thing you still know how to do, apart from the work you lost.
depth.question: What would you say to a friend who lost their money but not their mind?
